blocks.text: It remains to speak of the LXX Elders and the Vulgate translator, who render דוכיפת dukiphath as ἔποπα [epopa], upupa [hoopoe]. So also four Arabic translators, two printed and as many in manuscript, which I happened to compare with one another. For in all of them you will find الهدهد [al-hudhud] alhudhud, that is, the hoopoe. Many of the more recent scholars rightly follow this. For I hold the view that among many interpretations the most ancient is to be preferred, unless there are very weighty reasons for departing from it, and I see none such here. For why should Moses not have called the hoopoe the rock cock, the Chaldeans the mountain cock, the Rabbis the wild cock, when I see that the Greeks did the same? Thus Hesychius explains ἔποπα [epopa] as ἀλεκτρυόνα ἄγριον [alektryona agrion], and Aeschylus calls it πετραῖον ὄρνιν [petraion ornin], a rock bird (or even a rock hen). For we have shown in its place ^{b)} that ὄρνις [ornis] or ὄρνιθα [ornitha] is taken more specifically for the gallinaceous kind. The passage of Aeschylus to which we alluded is cited thus by the Philosopher, History, book 9, chapter 49:

Τοῦτον δ᾽ ἐπόπτην ἔποπα τῶν αὑτοῦ κακῶν Πεποικίλωκε, κ᾽ ἀποδηλώσας ἔχει Θρασὺν πετραῖον ὄρνιν ἐν παντευχίᾳ. [Touton d᾽ epoptēn epopa tōn hautou kakōn pepoikilōke, k᾽ apodēlōsas echei thrasyn petraion ornin en panteuchia.]
Which a great man renders thus:
He made him a hoopoe, to be himself the witness of his own crimes, with variegated body, a winged dweller of the rocks, fierce in his array. [col. 346]

The subject is Tereus, whom he calls the ἐπόπτην [epoptēn], or overseer, of his own evils, alluding to the name ἔποψ [epops], or hoopoe, into which Tereus was changed and became a πετραῖος ὄρνις [petraios ornis], a rock bird, or hen if you prefer. What of the fact that even today the common people of the Greeks call the hoopoe ἀγριοκόκορον [agriokokoron], wild cock? It is called a cock on account of its crest, although in the cock the crest consists of cartilage, in the hoopoe of feathers. Further, why it is called mountain, wild and rock bird is not obscure, since [III, 111] it usually dwells on mountain ridges, steep cliffs and the recesses of forests. The Philosopher, History, book 1, chapter 1: Τὰ δ᾽ ὄρεια (ζῶα), ὥσπερ ἔποψ [Ta d᾽ oreia (zōa), hōsper epops]: Some animals are mountain-dwellers, like the hoopoe. And book 9, chapter 11: Ἔνιοι δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσι καὶ τῇ ὕλῃ κατοικοῦσιν, οἷον ἔποψ [Enioi de tōn ornithōn en tois oresi kai tē hylē katoikousin, hoion epops]: Among birds there are some that inhabit mountains and forests, like the hoopoe. Aeschylus, in the passage cited above:

Ἀστῆ δὲ μισεῖ, τῶν δὲ Παλλήνης τόπων Δρυμοὺς ἐρήμους καὶ πάγους κατοικέει. [Astē de misei, tōn de Pallēnēs topōn drymous erēmous kai pagous katoikeei.] But it hates cities, and in the land of Pallene it dwells in the wilds of the groves and the ridges of the rocks.

Aelian writes the same, History, book 3, chapter 26: that hoopoes ὑποπλέκειν τὰς καλιὰς ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις, καὶ τοῖς πάγοις τοῖς ὑψηλοῖς [hypoplekein tas kalias en tais erēmois, kai tois pagois tois hypsēlois], build their nests in deserts and on lofty rocks. You see, therefore, reader, whoever you are, that this bird is rightly called דוכיפת, or rock cock.

But also, if one prefers to interpret דוכיפת dukiphath as the portentous or ominous and augural cock, the reason will be plain at once to anyone who looks at the hoopoe, whose appearance is so portentous that no one who sees this bird fails to be astonished. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 6, Fable 7:
— — on whose head a crest stands up, an immoderate beak juts out with a very long point; the bird's name is epops; its face seems armed.
Accordingly in Aristophanes' Birds, Euelpides, struck by this sight, exclaims thus:

Ὦ Ἡράκλεις, τοῦτο τί ποτ᾽ ἐστὶ θηρίον; Τίς ἡ πτέρωσις; τίς ὁ τρόπος τῆς τριλοφίας; [Ō Hērakleis, touto ti pot᾽ esti thērion? Tis hē pterōsis? tis ho tropos tēs trilophias?] By Hercules, what new kind of beast is this? Feathered with what manner of triple crest?
Τὸ ῥάμφος ἡμῖν σου γέλοιον φαίνεται, [To rhamphos hēmin sou geloion phainetai,] We see that your beak is ridiculous.

I pass over the fact that some write that the hoopoe, in the ancient superstition of magicians and augurs, was among the foremost of the birds of omen. The Arabic Pandectarius tells the fable that the stone Quirin betrays secrets and stirs up fantasies if it is placed on the breast of a sleeper, and that it is found in the nest of the hoopoe, which, he says, is wholly a bird of sorcery and augury, as magicians and augurs report. According to Isidore, Origins, book 12, chapter 7: If anyone going to sleep anoints himself with its blood, [III, 112] he will see demons choking him. Damir has much of this sort in the chapter On the properties of the hoopoe: that by fumigation with this or that part of it harmful things are driven from a dovecote; demons are cast out of the body; a man who has been bound by a spell against his marriage and devotatus [bewitched], to use Apuleius' word, is released; that eating its roasted heart with rue sharpens the wit and stirs the memory; that by hanging up its feathers one wins a lawsuit. He also prescribes various love-potions from the same bird, and likewise drugs by which enemies may be removed, places made desolate, eyes knocked out, and other such superstitious, vain, impious and — ἄῤῥητ᾽ ἀμείνω [arrhēt᾽ ameinō] things. Alkazuinius treats this same subject in such a way that he scarcely yields to Damir. From this it is clear that the magicians held the hoopoe in the highest wonder as a prodigious animal.
